video_title: Vincent Deluard: Why the Stock Market Is More Fragile Than You Think
gist: Vincent Deluard (StoneX) turns bearish on US stocks, citing weak breadth, near-zero stock correlation that suppresses the VIX, stagflation with a roughly $150-200 shadow oil price and consumption propped by asset drawdowns. He argues Europe is Japan 2011-12 but uglier, so a chaotic French-led debt crisis weakens the euro, and favors long yen, Korean won and UK equities.

themes.theme: US equity fragility and turning bearish

insights.claim: More than 70% of US stocks are below their 200-day moving average while the index made a new all-time high, a technical divergence Deluard expects to resolve with the top falling toward the bottom, and he is turning bearish on stocks after a 17-year bull market.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Narrow index leadership with weak breadth raises the odds of a correction or bear market.

insights.claim: Deluard expects equities may stay supported until the Anthropic IPO and the midterms, but sees the AI narrative as tiring with cracks accumulating and no replacement leadership.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: The Anthropic IPO is flagged as a possible sentiment peak for the AI trade.

insights.claim: About a third of US stocks trade at negative beta and average single-stock correlation to the index is around 5%, which Deluard calls unprecedented and attributes to pod-shop pair trades, the AI trade and macro-like earnings trading.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Near-zero correlation is suppressing index volatility and masking underlying stress.
insights.quote: We have about a third of US stocks traded trading at negative beta.

insights.claim: Recomputing the VIX with a normal 50-60% stock correlation gives a 'shadow VIX' of about 40, versus the actual VIX, because the correlation component of portfolio variance has collapsed to near zero.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: The VIX understates risk; any correlation normalization implies a volatility spike and likely a correction or bear market.

insights.claim: The MOVE index is at an all-time high while the VIX is normal, a breakdown in their usual close correlation, and Deluard expects it to resolve with bond volatility easing somewhat and equity volatility rising.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Equity vol is mispriced relative to rate vol; long-vol or hedging has asymmetric payoff.
insights.quote: it's very hard for stocks to rally when the VIX is above 20.

insights.claim: The summer was a churning market with rotating themes (refiners, tobacco, chips, back to AI), which Deluard reads as lack of conviction; he likes health care but its S&P 500 weight is near an all-time low so a rotation cannot carry the index.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: No sector has the weight to replace tech as the index driver, so rotation will not prevent an index drawdown.
insights.quote: you don't get a bull market with with refiners.

insights.claim: The S&P's September-October seasonal weakness is a statistical artifact of a few nasty bear markets that all occurred around midterm elections, and Deluard names the midterms a catalyst, expecting a blue sweep (betting pools near 70%).
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Midterm timing adds event risk to the weak-breadth setup.

themes.theme: Stagflation, tax receipts and the consumer

insights.claim: Deluard tracks nominal income through personal income tax collections rather than GDP or PMIs, noting growth jumped from roughly 4-5% before COVID to 6-8% afterward and has slowed this year from about 8-9% to near 5%.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Real-time tax receipts are a cleaner read on nominal growth and show it decelerating.
insights.quote: What I believe in is income, and the best way to track income is to look at tax collections

insights.claim: He gives four hypotheses for the post-COVID nominal growth boom: understated inflation, a roughly 6% of GDP deficit at full employment, a tech capex cycle near 3% of GDP, and productivity, with the answer a mix of all four.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: The nominal boom rests on fiscal and capex supports that may fade.

insights.claim: Real wages have been negative for four months as wages fully absorbed the oil shock, and consumption has held up only because people draw down investment accounts and 401(k)s, citing a JP Morgan study and Vanguard emergency-withdrawal data.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Consumption funded by asset drawdowns depends on the stock market, creating a reflexive risk.

insights.claim: Deluard sees a 2006-07 parallel with oil above 100, rising yields, a very low savings rate and consumption funded by asset harvesting, and says the sole justification for the bull market is the bull market itself.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: If the equity wealth effect reverses, consumption has little cushion.
insights.quote: Eventually the the sole justification for the bull market is the bull market itself.

insights.claim: Widening credit spreads in consumer sectors while yields rise contradict the narrative that higher yields reflect a growth shock, which would tighten spreads.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Spread damage in consumer names signals stress, not strength, behind higher yields.

insights.claim: The Bay Area economy is bifurcated even within the top of the K: Anthropic-type winners pull the market while workers at Salesforce and Adobe-like companies see falling stock packages and home prices, and Deluard says the 401(k)-maxing tech services class is starting to struggle.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Software-sector wage and equity-comp weakness may be a leading indicator for the affluent consumer.

themes.theme: Shadow oil, China PPI and the inflation outlook

insights.claim: With the Strait of Hormuz shut or quasi-shut for months, oil was held down by high global inventories, a strategic petroleum reserve release (low near 250 million barrels) and collapsed Chinese imports; Deluard says all of these are now running out as the SPR nears minimum operational level and Chinese buying returns.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Buffers that capped oil are exhausted, raising upside risk to prices.

insights.claim: Adding roughly $20 of refining margin and $20 of transport and insurance to WTI, the effective price paid for refined products in Asia implies a world of $150 to $200 oil, which Deluard calls the 'shadow' oil price.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Headline WTI understates the inflation impulse hitting the global economy.
insights.quote: we are living in a $150 to $200 oil uh world.

insights.claim: Chinese PPI is the leading global inflation indicator and is now running at 5-6% while the PBOC lets the yuan rise about 0.5% a month, reversing the Chinese PPI deflation that pulled global inflation down after 2022.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Imported goods inflation from China is turning from disinflationary to inflationary for Amazon and Walmart-type retail.
insights.quote: the leading indicator of inflation globally is Chinese PPI

insights.claim: Deluard cannot predict the next shock but says it will be inflationary because the policy reaction will be, since shocks are neutral and COVID produced deflation in China but 10% inflation in the US because of checks and supply mismanagement.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Inflation is best forecast from policy reaction functions, which currently lean toward stimulus (he cites a proposed $5,000 check).
insights.quote: I don't know what the next shock will be, but I know it will be inflationary because the policy reaction will be inflationary.

insights.claim: Agriculture is the most concentrated spillover risk: diesel and fertilizer shocks (fertilizers stuck in the Middle East), grains up 25-30% this year, a strong El Nino, a European drought that turned France into a grain importer and Black Sea grain stuck, which could turn the energy shock into a cultural shock in 2027.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Food prices drive political instability in import-dependent, dollar-short countries such as Egypt and Pakistan.
insights.quote: we're three meals away from from anarchy

insights.claim: Tariffs are a fiscal issue: after the Supreme Court decision and the war, tariff revenue was negative this summer from refunds of emergency tariffs, leaving the deficit about $500 billion above CBO estimates, so Deluard expects tariffs, export bans and similar measures to be the easiest lever.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Fiscal pressure pushes policy toward further tariffs and energy export curbs, both inflationary.

insights.claim: He sees no Fed put or fiscal put in the next two years, expecting a blue wave to bring investigations and impeachment gridlock in a 1970s-style stagflationary period where no one can fix the problem.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: The usual policy backstops for asset prices may be absent in the coming drawdown.
insights.quote: I don't see any of these puts in the next 2 years.

themes.theme: Bonds, term premium and inflation measurement

insights.claim: Rising bond yields are normalization after a decade of negative term premiums and QE, with 5.2% plausible given about 4% inflation, 2% real growth and AI capex of 3% of GDP.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: The prior zero-rate baseline was the anomaly, so yields may not fall back meaningfully.

insights.claim: Deluard is turning bullish on bonds mainly because he is bearish on stocks, preferring the belly of the curve where 5%-plus coupons give a buffer even if yields keep rising.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: He is flipping from no duration and overweight equities to adding duration and cutting equities.

insights.claim: Real yields near 3.5% with unmoved breakevens suggest the market is pricing the risk that CPI and PCE will be systematically understated or tampered with, so the rise in yields is not all real, which he says is not bad for gold and Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Gold and crypto resilience despite high real yields may reflect a hedge against suppressed inflation data.

themes.theme: Europe as Japan, weak euro and French debt crisis

insights.claim: Europe today is where Japan was in 2011-12, only uglier, and the only remaining path is a much weaker currency, since fiscal, monetary and productivity fixes failed in Japan and are failing in Europe.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: A structurally weaker euro is the base case for European macro positioning.
insights.quote: Europe today is where Japan was in 2011-12, just uglier.

insights.claim: Europe faces a negative productivity shock from costlier energy, Chinese competition crushing industrial exports and rising dependency ratios, so productivity reports from Lisbon to Draghi cannot fix it and immigration lacks political support.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Growth-led escapes are closed, leaving currency depreciation and financial repression.

insights.claim: Unlike Japan's engineered three-arrow weakening of the yen, Europe will get a weaker euro chaotically through a sequence of crises, first French debt, then probably Germany, with the euro possibly heading to 0.8, because 17-country coordination, 4% inflation and a US obsessed with trade balances block a clean devaluation.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Expect volatility and contagion rather than a smooth depreciation.
insights.quote: It's going to be a chaotic sequence of crisis that will eventually uh get get the euro much much weaker

insights.claim: France fits every marker of a sovereign debt crisis: high debt, a big primary deficit financed by foreigners in a currency it cannot print, no growth and unpopular politicians who cannot raise taxes or cut spending, and its R minus G is the most negative among major economies.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: French sovereign stress is the leading edge of the European crisis sequence.
insights.quote: We hit every single marker of a severe debt crisis.

insights.claim: Japan is exiting its debt trap: tax collection has grown 7% a year for ten years, so with rates at 4% R minus G stays very negative, and Japanese managers repatriating money is part of the pain in French bonds.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Supports a long-yen view and flags Japanese repatriation as a driver of European bond selling.

insights.claim: Deluard likes Asian currencies, specifically long yen as a hedge against a stock selloff, and long Korean won against the euro, which was up 15% in the past month.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Long-yen is a defensive hedge while long won/short euro is a terms-of-trade trade.

insights.claim: South Korea and Taiwan run current account surpluses around 25% of GDP expected to persist through 2030, with Samsung earning about a billion dollars a day, and Deluard argues this flood will leak into consumption, public investment and military spending, pressuring rates and currencies.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Memory-chip windfalls support won strength and eventually higher Korean rates.
insights.quote: Samsung makes a billion dollar a day.

insights.claim: Deluard proposes a rates trade of receiving Korean rates (he expects the Bank of Korea to be forced to hike as inflation, consumption and investment pick up) against paying European rates (the ECB cannot hike during a debt crisis).
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Offers a relative-value rates expression of the Korea-versus-Europe divergence.

insights.claim: If Europe copies Japan's playbook, the currency-hedged Japan ETF (DXJ) analog applies (long index, short currency); Deluard hesitates to buy European equities because the debt crisis worsens, though French luxury multiples (Hermes, LVMH) have halved and could eventually be worth buying.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: A hedged-Europe ETF is a possible later trade; not yet.

insights.claim: He favors the UK as a first-mover: UK defined benefit pensions cut domestic equity from about 50% to 5% in 20 years, MSCI UK is about 2% of global market cap (below its share of GDP), the budget is improving, and the UK would benefit from Eurozone debt stress, suggesting long UK versus short Eurozone equities.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Forced institutional selling and neglect make UK equities an under-owned relative-value pair trade.
insights.quote: the average uh defined benefit pension fund in the UK they used to have 50% in domestic stocks 20 years ago. Now it's down to 5%.

insights.claim: LatAm elections followed the same script in Chile, Colombia, Peru and Brazil (hard left versus hard right, tightening, then a late breakout for a pro-business right-wing candidate), but local managers have been taking profits after roughly 30% gains while foreigners with near-zero exposure may take over as buyers.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: A shift from local to foreign buying plus currency effects could extend EM outperformance, though political disappointment history argues for caution.

insights.claim: Crypto ownership by share of population is highest in South Korea (about 20%) then the US (about 15%), Taiwan, Brazil and Mexico, and the Korean number is real because law requires registering crypto accounts.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Korea is the marginal retail crypto buyer and a key liquidity source.

insights.claim: Deluard suggests recycling of Korea's chip-driven surpluses through bonuses at SK Hynix and other chipmakers into a gambling-prone, leverage-loving retail culture may explain crypto's resilience despite rising real yields and likely Democratic gains, and expects at least three more years of such surpluses.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Memory-cycle profits could be a multi-year tailwind for crypto flows.
